event: Amy's table has a place card at every seat, each name in her small even hand.
Natalie finds hers and sits where it tells her.
She'd never assign seats at her own table, but sees why Amy has: nobody hovers.
No dance by the chairs, no deferring or switching; everyone finds a name and sits.
Zadi holds hers up: "You made place cards."
Amy did: Zadi sits across from her so Amy can tell if she stops eating.
"I don't stop eating." "I know. It's one of the things I like about you."
The kitchen is warm and very clean, everything not dinner already put away.
The soup comes first: a squash soup better than Amy will admit.
Zadi says so at length.
Amy says the recipe is on a card in a box, and Zadi can have it.
Then a plate of greens, then the main, each in its turn, in the order Amy decided.
A card on the sideboard lists the whole meal top to bottom like an itinerary.
Each time a plate goes out, Natalie sees Amy check it and go still when the evening matches.
Zadi demands the truth: was there a seating diagram?
"I had a diagram," Amy says, as if it's the plainest thing in the world.
Zadi loves that about her.
Amy: Zadi laughs every month, then eats in the right order and goes home happy.
Zadi laughs; Natalie doesn't quite: she has spent many years feeding people.
Natalie starts to get up with her empty soup bowl.
Amy, not turning from the counter: "Leave it."
Natalie says she can carry a bowl; Amy: everything's handled, sit and be a guest.
So Natalie sits, a guest, and watches Amy run the dinner she built.
It's strange for her to sit with empty hands while someone else does the feeding.
At her own table she's never still; here Amy has carried it all already, in her head.
Cork coasters sit squared at every place; Natalie sets her glass on hers.
She catches Amy clocking it, and they let it pass without a word.
By the door, containers are already stacked with Natalie's and Zadi's names taped on.
The leftovers were portioned out before the meal was half eaten.
The main is chicken done with lemon; Natalie says twice that it's good.
Amy nods, pleased, and asks if anyone wants more before there isn't any.
Zadi empties the basket of good store bread.
Amy brings out a second loaf already bagged on the counter, bought in case. It was needed.
Zadi: the best she's eaten in weeks; she's been living on toast and self-pity.
Amy knows about the toast: there's a container by the door with Zadi's name on it.
Natalie asks Zadi how the reading is, knowing she's run dry.
It isn't: nothing has caught her since the blue one.
She's been rereading a cookbook for the pictures, a low place to be.
Amy says nothing to that.
Amy clears the plates, stacked and in order.
She comes back with a book and sets it by Zadi's coffee.
She saw it at the used place last week; she doesn't know if it's good, but it looked like Zadi.
Zadi turns it over and is quiet a second.
"Thank you," she says, smaller than the voice she's used all night.
Decaf comes at the end, in cups Amy set out before anyone arrived.
The itinerary on the sideboard comes down to its last line, then to nothing, every item met.
Amy reads the finished card, looks for the next thing to do, and finds none.
Then she sits down, pours herself the last of the coffee, and sits back with it.
The talk goes looser: the cold coming on, a neighbour's dog, last year's squash.
Amy puts in a word here and there and mostly listens.
The card behind her is done, with nothing left on it to do.
Her coffee cools at her elbow, forgotten.
Outside, sleet has come on, half rain, half snow, ticking at the dark glass.
None of them moves to go out into it yet.
